sections.title: First aid
sections.line: Treat small injuries yourself when help is slow to come.

items.name: A stocked first aid kit
items.why: Cuts, burns and sprains still happen when clinics are closed.
look: Sterile gauze pads in 2-inch and 4-inch sizes, roller bandages, triangular bandages and adhesive tape.
Non-latex exam gloves, scissors, tweezers and a thermometer.
Antibiotic ointment, a hot and cold compress, and bandages in assorted sizes.

items.name: A first aid manual on paper
items.why: Paper works with no power at all.
look: FEMA lists a first aid kit “and manual”. Keep the two together.

items.name: Spare medicines
items.why: Pharmacies may be closed or out of stock for days.
look: A supply of each prescription, plus pain relievers, anti-diarrhea medicine, antacids and laxatives.
Replace anything past its date. Check the whole kit once a year.

sections.title: Drinking water
sections.line: Water comes first. Store some, and have a way to make more safe.

items.name: Stored water
items.why: One gallon per person per day, for drinking, food and washing. Two weeks if you can.
look: Commercially bottled water is the safest. Keep it sealed and watch the use-by date.
For your own water, use food-grade storage containers. Not milk or juice jugs, and not glass.

items.name: A water filter
items.why: Removes dirt, parasites and some bacteria from water you collect.
look: Absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller, rated to NSF Standard 53 or 58 for cyst reduction.
Filters can’t remove viruses. Boil or disinfect the water too.

items.name: Plain unscented bleach and a dropper
items.why: A few drops make clear water safe when you can’t boil it.
look: Regular, unscented chlorine bleach. The label should say 6% or 8.25% sodium hypochlorite.
Not scented, color-safe, or with added cleaners. Less than a year old.
8 drops of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25%, per gallon. Wait 30 minutes.

sections.title: Food preparation and preservation
sections.line: Eat what you stored, cook without the grid, and keep food safe.

items.name: Food that keeps, and a manual can opener
items.why: At least several days of food that needs no fridge.
look: Non-perishable food your household already eats. Include a manual can opener and utensils.
Ready-to-eat canned food and high-energy foods like peanut butter and crackers.

items.name: A fridge and freezer thermometer
items.why: Tells you what to keep and what to throw out after the power goes off.
look: Throw out perishable food that sat above 40°F for two hours or more.

items.name: A camp stove and fuel
items.why: Cook and boil water when the stove at home doesn’t work.
look: A small cooking stove with a can of its fuel.
Outdoors only. Never use a camp stove, grill or generator indoors.

items.name: A pressure canner
items.why: Preserves a harvest for months without a freezer.
look: Low-acid foods must be processed in a pressure canner.
A dial gauge needs checking for accuracy every year. A weighted gauge doesn’t.

sections.title: Critical repairs
sections.line: Stop the damage from getting worse until help arrives.

items.name: A wrench to turn off utilities
items.why: A gas leak or a burst pipe can’t wait for a plumber.
look: A wrench or pliers that fit your gas and water shutoffs. Learn how before you need it.
For gas, a non-sparking wrench. Only a licensed technician should turn the gas back on.

items.name: Duct tape, plastic sheeting and a tarp
items.why: Seal a broken window, cover a damaged roof, or shelter in place.
look: Plastic sheeting, scissors and duct tape.
A tarp for a damaged roof, to stop more damage.

items.name: A fire extinguisher
items.why: Fire crews may be far away or busy.
look: At least an A-B-C type, for most home fires.
A “UL Listed” label. The largest size you can use safely and comfortably.

sections.title: Power
sections.line: Light, charge and stay safe when the grid is down.

items.name: Flashlights and extra batteries
items.why: Use them instead of candles.
look: One flashlight for every person in the house.
Extra batteries in the sizes they take.

items.name: A backup battery for your phone
items.why: Keeps a phone charged for calls, texts and alerts.
look: Chargers and a backup battery, kept charged.
A solar charger can top it up during a long outage.

items.name: Carbon monoxide alarms
items.why: Generators, stoves and heaters make a gas you can’t see or smell.
look: Battery backup. One in a central place on every level of the home.

items.name: A generator, used safely
items.why: Runs a fridge, a pump or medical equipment through a long outage.
look: Outdoors only, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages.
Plug appliances in with heavy-duty extension cords.
Never connect it to the house wiring unless a licensed electrician installs an approved transfer switch.

sections.title: General emergency preparedness
sections.line: The basics for any emergency, kept together and ready to grab.

items.name: A weather radio
items.why: Hear warnings and news when phones and internet are down.
look: Battery-powered or hand-crank, and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert.
NOAA Weather Radio needs a radio made to receive it.

items.name: A whistle and dust masks
items.why: Signal for help, and filter dusty or smoky air.
look: A whistle to signal for help, and a dust mask to help filter contaminated air.

items.name: Containers that carry it all
items.why: If you have to leave fast, the kit goes with you.
look: Items in airtight plastic bags, in one or two easy-to-carry bins or a duffel bag.
A waterproof container for copies of documents, and one for matches.

items.name: Warm bedding
items.why: Heat may be off for days.
look: A sleeping bag or warm blanket for each person.
A change of clothes for your climate and sturdy shoes.
